title: Hysteresis and dwell
physicalPurpose: Keep stored food below its temperature limit without damaging the compressor through excessive starts.
principalTechnique: Hysteresis and minimum on/off dwell protection
objective: Compare single threshold, hysteresis, and dwell protection on the same cold-storage room, then select the simplest configuration that meets the common temperature and transition criteria, while separately proving whether the dwell candidate enforces its declared minimum durations.

simplifications: The room and stored product are represented by one well-mixed thermal state.
Door load changes the no-cooling equilibrium from 4 to 6 degC.

The three-run comparison injects no stochastic sensor noise so its single-threshold case exactly reproduces the Lesson 2 baseline; the focused state-memory sequence uses declared deterministic temperatures.
Door timing is owned by the ST experiment clock, not absolute simulator startup time.

baseline.limitation: The Lesson 2 single threshold switches on every noisy crossing and can short-cycle the compressor.

change.decision: Use separate 2.50 degC on and 1.50 degC off thresholds, then require eight complete seconds before an opposite transition.

disturbances: The door opens at 60 s and closes at 90 s

acceptance.window: complete 120 s run including initial safe-off transition

abortPredicates: PV leaves the -10 to 10 degC experiment range
safety.restorationMode: Auto disabled with compressor demand at 0%
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Simulated cycling shall not be presented as physical compressor endurance evidence.

video.viewerOutcome: Explain why hysteresis needs retained state and why dwell protection is a separate equipment constraint.

learning.context: The same cold-storage plant now has automatic ON/OFF control, but Lesson 2 exposed sensor-driven chatter and excessive starts.
learning.reason: The compressor needs protection without pretending that a binary actuator can hold one exact temperature.
theory: Hysteresis uses separate ON and OFF thresholds and retains the previous requested state inside the band.
The resulting temperature cycle is a limit cycle, not numerical noise or a failure to converge.
Minimum on-time and off-time protect equipment independently of the temperature band.
Hysteresis reduces switching in this comparison; dwell enforces minimum state times and increases temperature movement even when the total switch count is unchanged.
learning.workedPrediction: At SP 2.00 degC and width 1.00 degC, cooling starts at 2.50 degC and stops at 1.50 degC; a demand to reverse before 8 s exposes a requested/applied mismatch until dwell is complete.
practicalPreparation: Retain the same plant, seed, door event, initial state, and limits for all three runs.
Predict thresholds, output state inside the band, and which transitions dwell will postpone.
learning.baseline: Use the retained Lesson 2 single-threshold result as the baseline with matching room, initial state and simulator-relative door event.
learning.change: Run the delivered hysteresis-with-dwell project, then compare its observations with the three retained cases; the project has no case selector.
learning.comparison: Compare temperature range, switch count, and shortest on/off durations without changing the plant or disturbance.
learning.validation: Verify binary MV, both thresholds, state retention inside the band, observable requested/applied mismatch, every completed dwell of at least 8 s, and the separate 3 degC door-event criterion.
learning.explanation: Explain why the same 2.00 degC PV can produce different MV values depending on the retained direction of travel.
learning.transfer: Choose a defensible hysteresis band and dwell boundary for another binary thermal actuator, and name the equipment data still needed for physical use.
